interviewQuestions.question: How would you structure a mobile app's architecture at the whole-app level, beyond any single screen's MVVM or MVI pattern?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate concerns into three layers with a strict, one-directional dependency rule: **presentation** (UI plus view models, rendering data and forwarding user actions, containing minimal business logic), **domain** (use cases encoding business rules, independent of both UI and data-source details), and **data** (repositories abstracting away whether something comes from network, local database, or cache).

The rule that actually matters is the dependency direction: presentation depends on domain, domain depends on abstractions the data layer implements — never the reverse, and never presentation reaching directly into a network client bypassing domain rules. A concrete test for whether this is actually working: can I swap the data layer's implementation (mock it for tests, or swap the local database technology) without touching domain or presentation code? If yes, the layering is real; if every change ripples across layers, it's layering in name only.

Within the presentation layer, I'd pick MVVM or MVI as the specific pattern for how one screen's state is organized — these aren't competing with the whole-app layering, they operate inside it. I'd also modularize by feature once the app is large enough to justify it, so module boundaries are compiler-enforced rather than a convention that erodes as the team grows.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about architecture at the right altitude — the whole app's structure, not just one screen's pattern.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Design the module structure for a mobile e-commerce app with browsing, cart, checkout, and account features, expecting the engineering team to grow from 5 to 30 over the next two years.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd split into feature modules aligned to those product areas — `browsing`, `cart`, `checkout`, `account` — each a separate build target with an explicit public interface and everything else genuinely private. I'd also pull out a small `core` module for things every feature genuinely needs: the network client, auth token handling, common UI components, and shared domain-level types like a `Money` value type — kept deliberately narrow, since a bloated 'shared' module just relocates the God-object problem rather than solving it.

Cross-feature dependencies are the part I'd design most carefully: checkout genuinely needs to read the cart, so `checkout` depends on `cart`'s public interface — that's a legitimate, explicit dependency, not a violation. What I'd actively prevent is a *circular* dependency (cart needing something from checkout) or an *implicit* one (checkout reaching past cart's interface into its internals) — module visibility rules should make the second one a compile error, not a code review catch.

For a team scaling to 30 engineers specifically, I'd map modules roughly to team ownership boundaries where possible, so a given module has a clear owning team — that turns 'who approves this PR' and 'who do I ask about this behavior' into a lookup instead of tribal knowledge, which matters a lot more at 30 engineers than at 5.

I would NOT over-modularize on day one with 5 engineers — I'd start with fewer, larger modules aligned to the product areas that already exist, and split further as specific modules start showing build-time pain or team-ownership friction, rather than guessing the final shape upfront.

**Testing:** whether you can design module boundaries around both technical dependencies and team scaling, not just technical layering alone.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design

interviewQuestions.question: You join a team whose app has one massive shared repository class that every feature depends on, and every PR touching it takes days to review because so many features are affected. How would you propose fixing this without stopping feature work for months?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't propose a big-bang rewrite — that's exactly the kind of project that stalls feature work and risks introducing regressions across everything at once. Instead I'd propose an incremental extraction: pick the feature area causing the most review pain right now, define a narrow, purpose-built repository interface for just that feature's data needs, and migrate that one feature to call the new interface while the old God repository keeps serving everyone else during the transition.

Concretely, that means the new `OrderRepository` might initially just delegate to the same underlying network/database calls the God repository already makes — the win at this stage isn't new functionality, it's an enforced seam between one feature and everything else, so a change to order-related data no longer requires a review that touches every other feature's code path.

I'd repeat this pattern feature by feature, prioritized by whichever currently causes the most review friction or the most incidents, rather than trying to plan the final module graph upfront. Over several quarters the God repository shrinks to genuinely shared concerns (auth, a base network client) and eventually disappears as a bottleneck, without ever blocking feature delivery for an extended migration window.

I'd also propose a lightweight rule going forward — no new feature adds a method to the shared repository, it gets its own — so the problem stops growing while the extraction is in progress.

**Testing:** whether you can propose a realistic, incremental migration plan instead of an idealized rewrite that ignores delivery pressure.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Migration

interviewQuestions.question: A junior engineer on your team wants to apply full Clean Architecture — three layers, dependency inversion, a use case class per business rule — to a five-screen internal tool with two engineers and no plans to grow. How do you respond?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd push back gently, because architecture is a cost paid to prevent a *specific, concrete* future cost, and I don't think this app has that cost yet. Three strict layers with dependency inversion buys testability in isolation, swappable data sources, and safety against feature coupling as a team scales — real benefits, but ones that matter most when there are many engineers touching the code concurrently, or the business logic is complex enough to need isolated unit testing, or the data source is genuinely likely to change.

For a five-screen internal tool with two engineers and no growth plan, that overhead — the extra interfaces, the indirection when tracing a bug through three layers instead of one — is a real, ongoing cost with a much smaller corresponding benefit. I'd suggest a lighter structure: a straightforward MVVM split per screen, business rules kept in plain, testable functions or classes without necessarily formalizing a full domain layer with dependency-inverted interfaces for every single one.

What I would keep regardless of scale: even a small app benefits from *not* putting business logic directly in a view — that's cheap to do correctly from day one and costs little. The distinction I'd draw for the engineer is between disciplines that are cheap to apply everywhere (keep logic out of views, write testable functions) versus structural investments (full layering, module boundaries) that should scale with the app's actual size and growth trajectory, not be applied maximally as a default.

**Testing:** whether you can right-size architecture to context instead of treating a pattern as universally correct regardless of scale — a common miss even among engineers who know the patterns well.
